batch_notes: Nine Rust targets, 126 properties, no example pins in the batch; all bugs with a test already name a Hegel property, so the only open attributions were tera/1 (no test), toml/2-3 (no test) and three ttf-parser duplicates. Recurring shapes: (1) KNOWN-FAILURE properties come in two flavours that the pin tag conflates: genuinely narrowed ones (tar full_range, tiff rows_per_strip, ttf-parser set_variation, toml crlf, ulid out_of_range, time/2-3) and general properties that merely carry the label because they fail (textwrap hegel_fill_is_wrap_joined_with_line_ending, time/1 sunday_based_week_numbers_parse_back over arbitrary dates, ttf-parser glyph_index with a boosted U+FFFF); I tagged pin where the README or the generator narrows to the failing region and not for textwrap's general property. (2) Generators that gate around unpinned bugs (toml valid_document_display_is_byte_identical for toml/2 and toml/3, tar uid_gid excluding bit 63, time signed_durations skipping the time/2 case) are the only trace of those findings; the rubric's 'cites the bug id' criterion should probably read 'describes and gates around the bug', which is what I applied for toml/2-3. (3) The three ttf-parser duplicate records (status duplicate, no test) were attributed to the property that plausibly originally exposed the bug rather than to the pin, so a naive count would double-attribute those bugs; filter on status. (4) Rubric edge: several 'roundtrip' tests here are parse->display byte identity (toml, format preservation) rather than encode->decode value identity; both landed in roundtrip. (5) tera's arithmetic oracles use std i128/f64, which the rubric could read as external (stdlib) or model (arithmetic written in the test); I chose model-oracle because std arithmetic is not an independent template engine, whereas tera's string filters vs std to_uppercase were classed external. (6) unicode-normalization is entirely law/consistency based with no independent oracle except Hangul arithmetic; time is the opposite, a two-oracle design (calendar model plus jiff) where each property bundles dozens of assertions, so per-property counts understate its coverage.
